entities.summary:
Giovanni Gaetano Orsini, who ascended to the papacy as Nicholas III on November 25, 1277, after a protracted six-month conclave, was a scion of the powerful Roman Orsini family. His brief pontificate, spanning less than three years until his death on August 22, 1280, was nevertheless a period of assertive papal policy, fundamentally aimed at consolidating the temporal power of the Papal States and curtailing the hegemonic ambitions of King Charles I of Sicily (Anjou) in Italy. Nicholas III's strategic diplomatic and ecclesiastical maneuvers positioned the papacy as a significant political force amidst the intricate power struggles of late 13th-century Europe, establishing precedents for both papal temporal sovereignty and the controversial practice of nepotism.

Central to Nicholas III's achievements was the Treaty of Viterbo in 1277, through which he secured the crucial territories of Romagna and the Exarchate of Ravenna from Rudolf I of Germany, thereby definitively incorporating them into the Papal States and ending centuries of imperial claims. In 1278, he compelled Charles I of Anjou to relinquish his powerful vicariate of Tuscany and his senatorial office in Rome, effectively dismantling Angevin dominance in central Italy and restoring papal authority over the Eternal City. Furthermore, Nicholas III issued the influential bull *Exiit qui seminat* in 1279, a comprehensive clarification of the Franciscan Rule that sought to reconcile the contentious factions of Conventual and Spiritual Franciscans regarding the thorny issue of absolute poverty, though its long-term impact proved divisive.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Nicholas III's papacy was crucial in consolidating the Papal States' temporal power, notably through the acquisition of Romagna, and in curbing Angevin influence in central Italy. His policies set precedents for papal territorial expansion and political maneuvering against secular rulers, impacting the future trajectory of the papacy and Italian politics.
